stances.claim: The Constitution authorizes the President to declare a national emergency and Congress to grant him extraordinary powers under reasonable terms for abnormal conditions endangering lives or wellbeing (economic crisis, pestilence, epidemic, typhoon, earthquake) -- but Congress must clearly define the specific powers, which cannot breach due process, just compensation, free expression, or the rule of law as CJ Sereno has recently stressed.

David v Arroyo (May 3, 2006, Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez ponente) distinguishes three extraordinary presidential powers -- (1) calling-out power vs lawless violence/invasion/rebellion, (2) executive power to ensure faithful obedience to laws, and (3) emergency powers -- and these should not be confused with the more stringent power to declare martial law or emergency rule.

The Arroyo bill prudently restricts emergency-powers use to two years (unless sooner withdrawn by Congress) and subjects authorized negotiated infrastructure contracts to strict transparency and accountability conditions -- and Tugade's assurance that congressional + SC oversight will check abuses provides additional institutional safeguards.

Tugade's Davao powwow admonition to business leaders -- 'You expect us not to be corrupt? Can we expect you not to corrupt us?' -- captures the two-sided dynamic of corruption and rhymes with the closing aphorism that 'there are no bribe-takers, when there are no bribe-givers,' making demand-side corruption (bribe-givers) as much the problem as supply-side (bribe-takers).

The Integrity Summit jokes -- judge returning P50K to 'level the playing field' between two bribers; lawyer selling a Mercedes-Benz for P1,000 -- demonstrate 'the wrong way to level the playing field' and 'the wrong way to legalize a bribe,' showing that judicial corruption involves both judge-creativity and lawyer-creativity in mutually adapted forms.
stances.rhetorical_move: pedagogical-joke framing with explicit moral extraction

notable_anecdotes: The P2.4 billion DAILY traffic cost from the 2013 JICA study -- 'Repeat, daily' -- using the emphatic repeat to physicalize the magnitude.

Tugade's bilingual Davao admonition to top business leaders: 'You expect us not to be corrupt? Can we expect you not to corrupt us?' -- 'to the thunderous delight of the audience,' demonstrating Tugade's quip style and confronting demand-side corruption.

Judge-joke 1 in full preserved: the judge calling lawyers to chambers and saying 'Compañeros, both of you surreptitiously bribed me. You, counsel for the plaintiff, gave me P250,000 while you, counsel for the defendant, sent me P200,000. As an evenhanded and transparent judge, I will not allow anyone of you to unduly influence me. So, I am returning P50,000 to you counsel for the plaintiff. Now, after I have leveled the playing field, both of you can expect equal treatment from me.' -- CJ's signature judge-corruption joke with 'compañero' Spanish-tagalog register.

Judge-joke 2 in full preserved: the lawyer arriving home with a brand-new Mercedes-Benz on the judge's driveway, offering to sell it for P1,000; the judge replying 'In that case, I'll buy two, one for me and one for my wife.' -- the 'wrong way to legalize a bribe' canonical example.

Tugade as 'de campanilla' lawyer -- Spanish-loanword tagging meaning 'of the bell' (top-rank/illustrious) -- CJ's signature epithet for top-tier legal talent, paired with San Beda salutatorian credential.
The 'When the going gets tough, the tough gets going' aphorism applied to Tugade's traffic assignment -- using sports-folk-wisdom to convey assignment-difficulty acknowledgment.

The unscrupulous-client question: 'I do not care whether you know the law. My question is: Do you know the judge?' -- single sentence capturing demand-side judicial corruption in its most distilled form.
The closing aphorism: 'there are no bribe-takers, when there are no bribe-givers' -- clean inversion making the anti-corruption argument fully symmetrical.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban discusses former President and current Pampanga Rep. Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo's bill granting incoming President Duterte emergency powers to solve Metro Manila's traffic mess -- the 'crisis that bastardized our lives' costing P2.4 billion daily per a 2013 JICA study (repeat, daily). Eduardo Yap, MAP traffic czar, asked CJ weeks earlier whether the incoming President is clothed with emergency powers; CJ confirmed: under the Constitution, the President can declare a national emergency and Congress can grant extraordinary powers under reasonable terms for abnormal conditions endangering lives or wellbeing (economic crisis, pestilence, epidemic, typhoon, earthquake) -- but Congress must clearly define the specific powers, which cannot breach due process, just compensation, free expression, or the rule of law as CJ Sereno has stressed. CJ advised Yap to read and reread David v Arroyo (May 3, 2006), the landmark decision by Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez distinguishing three extraordinary presidential powers -- (1) calling-out power vs lawless violence/invasion/rebellion, (2) executive power to ensure faithful law-obedience, and (3) emergency powers -- not to be confused with the more stringent power to declare martial law. The Arroyo bill prudently restricts emergency-powers use to two years (unless sooner withdrawn) and subjects authorized negotiated infrastructure contracts to strict transparency and accountability conditions. Tugade -- a 'de campanilla' lawyer (class salutatorian at San Beda College of Law) -- assured that abuses would be checked by congressional + SC oversight. At the Cabinet's Davao powwow, Tugade admonished top business leaders: 'You expect us not to be corrupt? Can we expect you not to corrupt us?' -- to thunderous delight. The quip reminds CJ of the Integrity Summit (Sept 19, 2014) where he prefaced his anti-corruption-in-judiciary speech with two jokes: (1) a judge summons lawyers and announces 'Compañeros, both of you surreptitiously bribed me. You, counsel for the plaintiff, gave me P250,000 while you, counsel for the defendant, sent me P200,000. As an evenhanded and transparent judge, I will not allow anyone of you to unduly influence me. So, I am returning P50,000 to you counsel for the plaintiff. Now, after I have leveled the playing field, both of you can expect equal treatment from me' -- the wrong way to level the playing field; (2) a lawyer visits the judge offering to sell a brand-new Mercedes-Benz parked on his driveway for P1,000 -- the judge replies 'In that case, I'll buy two, one for me and one for my wife' -- the wrong way to legalize a bribe. These 'devilish games and witchcraft' impelled the Makati Business Club + European Chamber of Commerce 'Integrity Initiative,' and judges 'will not be bribed unless clients inveigle their lawyers to go beyond the outer limits of advocacy and soar to the stratosphere of corruption and malevolence' -- unscrupulous clients telling lawyers 'I do not care whether you know the law. My question is: Do you know the judge?' Closing aphorism: 'there are no bribe-takers, when there are no bribe-givers.'
